LISTEN FOR 0:43.85: handclaps on the right falling exactly between the hat's beats for one strip (2.7 s), then with the beats for the next, and so on, eight times: the claps come forward and sink back every 2.7 seconds, and each change is a seam of the strip.
THE REASON. In 'opposite' everything is read from both ends at once: the strip, by the two guitars; the meetings, by the bass and then the thumb. One thing is not: the count. The drummer's hat counts quarters in four straight through, from outside the strip. Read each strip's count from its far end, the way the right hand reads its notes (a stroke on tick t goes to tick 18 minus t), and because a strip is nineteen sixteenths long the answer is not the count again: on every other strip it falls exactly BETWEEN the beats, and on the strips between it falls exactly ON them. (The arithmetic: a beat at sixteenth b, in a strip that starts at a, is mirrored to 2a + 18 - b. Every b is a multiple of four, so the mirror is on a beat when 2a + 18 is, and the starts are nineteen apart: 2a + 18 is 18, 56, 94, 132 ..., a multiple of four every second strip.) So nothing was chosen but the rule the song already has. The seam of every strip, which nothing in the kit has ever marked, becomes that change.
THE PART IS CLAPPED: one pair of hands, right of centre (0.45), beside the guitar that reads backwards; the hat it answers is left of centre. No other song on the record has clapping hands (Carrying Capacity's drum machine has a clap voice, 22 strokes of it beside its snare: a circuit's clap, several bursts at once; this is one person's). Each clap is the mirror of one hat stroke, with the hat's accent mirrored too: 40 fall between the beats (strips 1, 3, 5 ... of the sixteen, counting from one) and 36 with the hat.
